lines.text: A university campus is a self-contained world with its own geography, vocabulary, and culture. The main academic buildings house lecture theatres (large tiered rooms for lectures), seminar rooms (smaller spaces for group discussions), laboratories (for science and engineering experiments), and tutorial rooms. The library is the intellectual heart of the campus — housing physical and digital collections, study spaces, computer clusters, and often a rare books archive. Student accommodation ranges from halls of residence (first-year dormitories) to shared houses and private flats. The students' union (SU) is both a representative body and a social hub, hosting societies, clubs, events, bars, and support services. Administrative buildings contain the registry (student records), the finance office (fees and funding), and the international office (visa and overseas student support). Sports facilities typically include a gym, swimming pool, sports pitches, and courts. The campus may also feature a chapel, a health centre, a careers service, and a counselling service. Navigation uses specific terms: 'the quad' (quadrangle — a courtyard), 'the precinct' (pedestrian area), 'blocks' and 'wings' (building sections). Academic staff include professors, senior lecturers, lecturers, and teaching assistants. Understanding campus vocabulary helps international students settle in quickly, navigate bureaucracy, and participate fully in university life.

lines.text: 'Oxbridge' is the collective term for Oxford and Cambridge — the UK's oldest and most prestigious universities. Their unique vocabulary includes 'college' (residential community), 'tutorial' (one-to-one teaching), 'Michaelmas term', and 'matriculation' (formal admission ceremony).

lines.text: The Russell Group is a collection of 24 leading UK research universities (including Manchester, Edinburgh, UCL, and King's College London). 'Russell Group university' is commonly used as a quality marker — equivalent to 'Ivy League' in American English.

lines.text: British degrees are classified: First (70%+, exceptional), 2:1 (60-69%, very good), 2:2 (50-59%, average), Third (40-49%, minimum pass). 'Getting a First' or 'a 2:1' is how British people describe their results. Many employers require a minimum 2:1.
